flagged:
AI-Generated (145 words): IFS has protective parts too, and it teaches people to approach them without shame or a fight, so "meet the protector first" fits right in.
My reparenting method diverges from IFS at an important point. In standard IFS, the healer is the Self, a calm, compassionate inner source that's supposed to be available once your parts "unblend." I emphasize the inner adult you build and practice occupying: Nurturer, Protector, and Leader, Guide, or Guru. That's still one grown-up with three jobs, like back in The Chicken-and-Egg Problem.
And if that calm Self never shows up for you? Remember letting the phone ring when you know how that call goes, back in The Parent You Inherited? That's borrowed adulthood, one grown-up job at a time until it's yours, and it works fine with no calm Self in sight.

AI-Generated (273 words): A grown-up you can trust gets built through care and boundaries, and through action and direction.
IFS calls these wounded young parts “exiles.” I find that pathologizing. I prefer to speak of a child who needs parenting and integration, rather than naming them by their wounded or excluded condition. IFS "unburdening," often done after witnessing a part's origin story, can be powerful. But it can also get dramatic, with a lot of focus on memories and plenty of room for suggestion, and that can knock people off balance, especially if they tend to dissociate (DID-like fragmentation included) or to spiritually bypass.
No bad parts, maybe, but an awful lot of them: managers, firefighters, exiles, polarized parts, legacy burdens, Self-energy, guides, new subparts... The map can turn into a maze. Some practitioners use the model gently, and others seem to leave people more fragmented while trying to fix the fragmenting. And having institutes and certifications behind a framework doesn't make it any truer, or safer for that matter.
Before choosing a therapist, get to know the strengths and pitfalls of IFS and reparenting. Could an IFS therapist help? They may, if they're skilled and grounded. You'd want one who's trauma-informed and doesn't put ideas in your head, especially one who understands dissociation. For your little one's pain, or for shame, a good reparenting therapist may fit better. The same goes for attachment wounds or abandoning yourself, or not having an inner adult you can count on.
